title: Muffin — Business lines
description: Revenue and operating income per disclosed business line, parsed from each filing's own XBRL instance. AGGREGATE WITHIN ONE partition ONLY — an axis can carry several overlapping splits that each sum to the consolidated total (Amazon's FY2025 10-K holds three, all 716,924,000,000), so summing an axis doubles the company's revenue and summing the table triples it. Every panel here reads `security_segment_current`, which serves partition 1 alone, or filters partition_id explicitly.

panels.title: Business lines — what is actually readable today
panels.description:
Every company whose filing has been parsed into a disclosed split, with the largest line.

ORDERED BY THE NUMBER OF LINES, NOT BY REVENUE. Revenue is in each filer's own currency, so sorting on it ranks by exchange rate — TSMC's TWD 3,272,600,000,000 outranks every US company while being nothing like the largest. `split_total` is safe because it is summed WITHIN one (company, axis), which is one currency by construction.

Reads `security_segment_spine` (materialised, refreshed hourly): the live view is 3.8 ms for one security and 6.1 s for all of them.

targets.rawSql:
select
  s.name as company,
  c.axis,
  count(*) as lines,
  max(c.currency_code) as currency,
  (array_agg(coalesce(c.concept_name, c.member_code) order by c.revenue desc nulls last))[1] as largest_line,
  max(c.revenue) as largest_line_revenue,
  sum(c.revenue) as split_total,
  max(c.period_ending) as period
from market.security_segment_spine c
join market.security s on s.security_id = c.security_id
where c.kind in ('product','business')
group by s.name, c.axis
order by count(*) desc, s.name

panels.title: Companies with a business-line breakdown
panels.description: Counted over SECURITIES, not rows. Read it beside the filings-parsed panel: this rising while filings-parsed is flat means nothing new is being read.

targets.rawSql: select count(distinct security_id) as value from market.security_segment

panels.title: Filings read for segments
panels.description: Filings whose XBRL instance has been parsed. A filed document is immutable, so this only ever goes up — unless `segment_parser.version` is bumped, which deliberately re-queues everything.

targets.rawSql: select count(*) as value from market.security_filing where segments_parsed_at is not null

panels.title: Filings still to read
panels.description:
The live backlog, PER REGULATOR. Both views are auto-sampled into `backlog_sample` like every other `pending_%` view, so the TREND is on the Pipeline dashboard — this is the current depth.

SPLIT DELIBERATELY. A single total cannot show that one regulator has stalled while the other drains: the sum keeps moving and the stalled half is invisible. Same reason the throughput panel below draws a series per resource rather than one line.

targets.rawSql:
select 'SEC' as metric, count(*) as value from market.pending_segments
union all
select 'DART (Korea)', count(*) from market.pending_kr_segments
union all
select 'NSE (India)', count(*) from market.pending_in_segments

panels.title: Filings with no XBRL to read
panels.description: Not a failure. XBRL became mandatory in phases from 2009, so a full history reaches thousands of filings that can never carry a segment — this counts what the submissions walk told us to skip rather than pay two requests to discover.

targets.rawSql: select count(*) as value from market.security_filing where is_xbrl = false

panels.title: Segment facts written per run
panels.description:
Throughput for every resource that reads a filing or writes a segment row — SEC (`security-segments`, `security-filing-history`, `security-filings`) Korea/DART (`security-kr-segments`, `kr-filings`) and India/NSE (`security-in-segments`, `in-filings`).

DELIBERATELY DRAWS ZEROS. A run that wrote nothing is the single most informative point on this chart — it is what a stalled resource looks like, and `written > 0` would hide exactly that.

THE RESOURCE LIST IS HARDCODED AND GUARDED. `check_dashboards_can_render.py` fails CI when a resource that upserts `security_segment` in `market-refresh/index.ts` is missing here, because a throughput panel that silently omits a regulator keeps drawing a healthy line for the other one — which is worse than not drawing it at all.

targets.rawSql:
select date_trunc('hour', started_at) as time, resource as metric, sum(written) as value
  from market.refresh_run
 where $__timeFilter(started_at)
   and resource in ('security-segments','security-filing-history','security-filings',
                    'security-kr-segments','kr-filings',
                    'security-in-segments','in-filings')
 group by 1, 2 order by 1

panels.title: Business lines nobody has mapped yet — the curation queue
panels.description:
A DRIFT COUNTER, not a work queue: `segment_alias` is EDITORIAL, so this is expected to be non-zero for ever and grows with every new filer parsed.

IT IS NOT RANKED BY HOW MANY COMPANIES USE THE MEMBER, and that is a measured fact rather than a preference. An XBRL extension member is minted in the filer's OWN namespace, so across the whole universe **320 extension members are used by exactly one issuer and ZERO by two** — `amzn:AmazonWebServicesMember` and `msft:IntelligentCloudMember` can never collide. The only members two companies share are the standard ones, and every one of those is geography, already resolved without curation. Ranking on that count put residual buckets at the head of the queue.

Ranked instead by FUND WEIGHT — a percentage, so free of currency, unlike revenue — with catch-alls demoted. `issuers` and `securities` are both shown because a dual-listed company is one company: TSMC's local line and its ADR made four `tsm:` members read as the queue's only cross-company overlap.

Catch-alls are FLAGGED, NOT FILTERED. "90% of this company is in a bucket called Other" is a real answer about disclosure quality, and a panel must not hide the state it exists to reveal.

targets.rawSql:
select
  q.member_code,
  q.kind,
  q.best_weight,
  q.largest_share_pct,
  q.issuers,
  q.securities,
  q.is_catch_all,
  q.largest_revenue,
  q.a_currency_code as currency,
  q.an_axis as axis
from market.pending_segment_alias q
order by q.is_catch_all, q.best_weight desc nulls last, q.largest_share_pct desc nulls last

panels.title: Can these companies actually be compared?
panels.description:
The question the feature is FOR: for each shared concept, how many companies disclose it. One company is not a comparison.

NO COMBINED REVENUE COLUMN, deliberately — it used to sum TWD, DKK and USD into one number and present it as a fact, which is the shape that once rendered Alibaba's CNY revenue as "$1.02T". A segment MARGIN is a percentage and is safe to average across currencies; `currencies` says how many are behind the row.

It is also the honest answer to "compare the iPhone with the Pixel": Alphabet does not disclose Pixel revenue (it sits inside Google other) and Samsung is not an SEC filer, so no amount of ingestion will make that row appear. AWS vs Google Cloud vs Intelligent Cloud does, because all three disclose it.

targets.rawSql:
select
  c.concept_name as concept,
  count(distinct c.security_id) as companies,
  round(avg(c.operating_margin_pct), 1) as avg_segment_margin_pct,
  round(avg(c.revenue_share_pct), 1) as avg_share_of_its_company_pct,
  count(distinct c.currency_code) as currencies
from market.security_segment_spine c
where c.concept_name is not null
group by c.concept_name
order by count(distinct c.security_id) desc, c.concept_name

panels.title: Weighted classification — where a single sector label is misleading
panels.description:
The Amazon case, generalised: companies whose profit is concentrated somewhere other than their headline sector. `weight` is the share of revenue or of operating income that a classification accounts for; a company appears here when the two disagree most.

These rows are ADDITIVE — they sit below yfinance in source priority and never change the sector a page puts in its header.

targets.rawSql:
select
  s.name as company,
  i.name as line,
  max(i.weight) filter (where i.source_code = 'segment-revenue') as revenue_weight,
  max(i.weight) filter (where i.source_code = 'segment-profit')  as profit_weight,
  round(abs(coalesce(max(i.weight) filter (where i.source_code = 'segment-profit'), 0)
          - coalesce(max(i.weight) filter (where i.source_code = 'segment-revenue'), 0)), 3) as gap
from market.security_industries i
join market.security s on s.security_id = i.security_id
where i.source_code in ('segment-revenue','segment-profit')
group by s.name, i.name
order by gap desc nulls last

panels.title: Splits that do NOT reconcile to the filing
panels.description:
The same arithmetic `check_segments_reconcile.py` runs in market-verify, drawn continuously. A split whose members do not sum to the company's own consolidated revenue means the parser lost a member, counted a subtotal, or partitioned a filing shape it has not seen.

EMPTY IS THE HEALTHY STATE, and that is why this panel has no floor and no limit: the first row to appear is the whole point.

targets.rawSql:
with split as (
  select g.security_id, g.axis, g.period_ending, g.period_type, sum(g.value) as total
    from market.security_segment_latest g
   where g.metric_code = 'revenue' and g.partition_id = 1
   group by 1,2,3,4
)
select s.name as company, split.axis, split.period_ending as period,
       split.total as split_total, m.value as filing_total,
       round(100 * (split.total - m.value) / nullif(m.value, 0), 2) as disagreement_pct
  from split
  join market.security s on s.security_id = split.security_id
  join market.security_metric m
    on m.security_id = split.security_id and m.metric_code = 'revenue'
   and m.period_type = split.period_type and m.as_of = split.period_ending
 -- 0.5%, matching segments.ts and check_segments_reconcile.py. Segment revenue
 -- carries a reconciling item (Alphabet's is 127,000,000 of hedging gains on
 -- 402,836,000,000 = 0.032%), so an exact test would list every large filer here.
 where abs(split.total - m.value) > greatest(1, abs(m.value) * 0.005)
   and abs(m.value) > 1000
 order by abs(split.total - m.value) desc

panels.title: Breadth — companies reached, against filings parsed
panels.description:
THE NUMBER THAT GATES THE FEATURE, and the one that was invisible while it was wrong. Until migration 156 `pending_segments` was ordered by fund weight — a property of the SECURITY — so the queue walked one company's entire 20-year history before starting the next. Measured 2026-08-29: 440 filings parsed, belonging to **14 securities** (69, 69, 69, 65, 61, 57, 39, 15, 10, 9, 9, 9, 8, 5 each) out of ~3,500 SEC filers.

Nothing could report it. `written` read as throughput, `remaining` fell, `ok` was true and the reconciliation guard passed — because the rows being written were CORRECT. They were the wrong rows first. The two lines diverging is the healthy shape; them moving together at a ratio of ~30:1 is the defect returning.

`showPoints: always` because these come from an hourly sampler: a timeseries draws a LINE, and a handful of points at the right-hand edge is indistinguishable from no data.

targets.rawSql:
select date_trunc('hour', u.sampled_at) as time,
       case u.metric when 'segments.companies' then 'companies reached'
                     else 'filings parsed' end as metric,
       max(u.value) as value
from market.universe_sample u
where $__timeFilter(u.sampled_at)
  and u.metric in ('segments.companies','segments.filings_parsed')
group by 1, 2 order by 1

panels.title: How deep is the queue into each company?
panels.description:
`round` is a filing's depth into its OWN company's history — round 1 is every filer's most recent annual report. Breadth-first means the queue drains round 1 across all filers before any company gets a second year.

PER REGULATOR, because that is the unit the ordering works in: SEC and DART have separate backlogs and separate resources, so a merged table would let a healthy SEC round 1 mask a Korean queue that has not started.

targets.rawSql:
with q as (
  select 'SEC' as regulator, security_id, round from market.pending_segments
  union all
  select 'DART (Korea)', security_id, round from market.pending_kr_segments
  union all
  select 'NSE (India)', security_id, round from market.pending_in_segments
)
select
  q.regulator,
  b.depth,
  count(*) as filings,
  count(distinct q.security_id) as companies
from q
cross join lateral (
  -- The bucket AND its sort key together: labelled buckets ordered by their own text put '21+'
  -- above '6-20', which reads as a queue that has skipped ahead.
  select case when q.round = 1 then 1 when q.round <= 5 then 2 when q.round <= 20 then 3 else 4 end as ord,
         case when q.round = 1 then '1 - latest annual, every filer'
              when q.round <= 5 then '2-5'
              when q.round <= 20 then '6-20'
              else '21+' end as depth
) b
group by q.regulator, b.ord, b.depth
order by q.regulator, b.ord

panels.title: Where each company earns — no curation required
panels.description:
Revenue by the geography a filer discloses. Every row here was readable WITHOUT anyone mapping anything: `country:US` is ISO 3166 and joins `market.countries`, and the standard region members (`srt:NorthAmericaMember`, `us-gaap:EMEAMember`) carry published labels. That is 41 of the 113 members that had been sitting in the curation queue.

A country is geography WHEREVER IT ARRIVES — TSMC files `country:TW` on the BUSINESS-segments axis, because its reportable segments are geographic. Reading the kind off the axis put it in the product queue.

`country_iso2` is null for a REGION: `us-gaap:NonUsMember` is everywhere-except-the-US, and pinning it to one code would file a whole company's foreign revenue under an arbitrary country.

THE AXIS COLUMN IS NOT DECORATION. A country can be disclosed on the geography axis AND appear as a segment of the same name on the business axis, with different numbers — measured live, one filer reports `country:US` at 149,617,000,000 (66.7% of its geographic split) and a business segment also called United States at 643,000,000 (0.25%). Both are real and neither is a duplicate of the other, but without the axis they read as the same row disagreeing with itself. 3 of 135 rows today; no company's shares sum above 100%, because a share is computed within its own axis.

targets.rawSql:
select
  s.name as company,
  g.member_label as place,
  g.country_iso2 as iso,
  g.axis,
  g.revenue,
  g.currency_code as currency,
  g.revenue_share_pct as share_of_its_axis_pct,
  g.period_ending as period
from market.security_segment_geography g
join market.security s on s.security_id = g.security_id
order by s.name, g.axis, g.revenue desc nulls last

panels.title: Segment spine refresh — milliseconds against the 8s ceiling
panels.description:
A TRIPWIRE, not a performance chart. `security_segment_spine` is materialised because the live aggregation is 6.1 s at 1.92M qualifying rows while a single-security read is 3.8 ms — so every whole-table reader was a few hundred thousand rows from `57014 canceling statement due to statement timeout` while every probe said the view was healthy. Fourth occurrence of that shape here.

The refresh is a PostgREST RPC, which is ONE statement under the role's **8,000 ms** timeout. Measured at 7,242 ms concurrent on 1.92M qualifying rows — and 38.3% of production's segment rows qualify, so that is roughly a 5M-row table. When this line approaches 8,000 the fix is the one migration 142 already established: give it a pg_cron job, which has no PostgREST timeout.

It is plotted because a number computed and thrown away cannot warn anybody — the same reason `refresh_log` was replaced by `refresh_run`.

targets.rawSql:
select date_trunc('hour', r.started_at) as time,
       'spine refresh' as metric,
       max((r.report->>'segment_spine_ms')::numeric) as value
from market.refresh_run r
where $__timeFilter(r.started_at)
  and r.resource = 'facets-refresh'
  and jsonb_typeof(r.report->'segment_spine_ms') = 'number'
group by 1 order by 1
